readerTitle: The $120,000 that was shrinking in the bank
caseNote: 가상 사례 (배관 서비스 업체, 마케팅 에이전시) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 남는 현금은 '안전하게 둘까, 불릴까'가 아니라 '언제 필요한 돈인가'로 나눈 뒤, 나중에 쓸 돈만 물가를 이기는 곳에 둔다.
misconception: 통장에 그냥 둔 현금은 위험이 없다. 여윳돈은 이율이 가장 높은 곳에 넣는 게 최선이다.

sources.text: 재무의 표준 개념 (명목 수익률·실질 수익률, 피셔 관계식의 근사, 유동성)

factChecks.note: 구매력 계산: $120,000 ÷ 1.03 = $116,505 (약 $116,500), 감소분 약 $3,500. 물가 상승률 3%는 설명용 가정이며 특정 국가·연도의 실제 수치가 아닙니다.
실질 수익률 ≈ 명목 수익률 − 물가 상승률은 근사식입니다. 정확한 식은 (1+명목)÷(1+물가)−1이며, 4%·3%일 때 약 0.97%입니다. 카드에는 "about 1%"로 적었습니다.
배관 업체: 월 비용 $30,000 × 3개월 = $90,000, 나머지 $30,000. 에이전시: 월 비용 $50,000, 고정 예치 제안 $150,000이면 남는 현금 $50,000(1개월분). 계산을 다시 확인하세요.
특정 금융상품·국가별 세금·예금보호 제도는 다루지 않았습니다. 중도 해지 수수료 등은 일반적인 설명으로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: The $120,000 that was shrinking in the bank
body: Dana runs a plumbing company with six vans. After a strong year, the business account holds $120,000. Monthly costs run about $30,000.
It feels like the safest money she has ever had. But sitting perfectly still, it is quietly getting smaller. And the obvious fix could make things worse.

image.label: A business bank balance slowly melting like an ice cube
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 배관공 작업 밴 옆에 통장 잔고 "$120,000"가 적힌 얼음 덩어리가 천천히 녹아 물방울이 떨어짐. 실제 은행·브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Dana do with the $120,000?
body: Dana has no debts. Work is steady, but winters are slower and a van can break down without warning.

options.text: Keep it all in the business account. Cash is safe.
options.feedback: She can reach every dollar today, which is real safety. But at no interest while prices rise, the money buys less each year. Inflation is eating her **real return**.

options.text: Keep about three months of costs ready, and put the rest where it earns more but can be reached within weeks
options.feedback: Each dollar is matched to when it might be needed. The ready cash covers **liquidity**, and the rest has a chance to beat inflation.

options.text: Put it all in a five-year fixed deposit with the highest rate
options.feedback: The best rate, but the money is **illiquid**. If a van dies in a slow winter, she may pay a penalty or borrow to reach her own cash.

cards.title: What one "safe" year does to $120,000.
body: The balance never moved. What it can buy fell by about **$3,500**, with no loss ever showing up on a statement.

breakdown.label: Start of year
breakdown.detail: In an account paying no interest

cards.title: Cash is not risk-free. It loses slowly.
body: Your **real return** is roughly what money earns minus how fast prices rise. An account paying 4% while prices rise 3% grows buying power by about 1%. An account paying 0% shrinks it by about 3%.
So idle cash carries a risk too. It is just quiet and certain instead of sudden. The goal for money you won't need soon is to earn more than inflation.

cards.title: Sort cash by when you'll need it.
body: **Liquidity** is how quickly you can turn something into cash without losing value. Higher returns usually ask you to give some of it up. So split the money by time:
list: **Ready:** the next one to three months of costs, reachable today
**Reserve:** shocks like a dead van or a lost client, reachable within weeks
**Long-term:** money you won't touch for years, free to earn more
cards.callout: Fill the buckets in this order. Only the last one should chase the highest rate.
cards.softwareNote: A subscription business that collects annual payments up front holds cash for service it still owes. That money belongs in the ready bucket, even though it looks like a surplus.

cards.title: Now it's a marketing agency.
body: You run a 12-person agency with $200,000 in the bank and monthly costs of $50,000. One client brings in 40% of revenue.
Your bank offers a much better rate if you lock $150,000 for three years. What do you do?

options.text: Take the offer. Three years of a better rate adds up.
options.feedback: You'd keep only one month of costs liquid. If the big client leaves, the locked money can't pay salaries while you replace them. A **liquidity** problem can sink a profitable firm.

options.text: Keep a reserve big enough to survive losing that client for several months, and lock only what's left
options.feedback: The reserve is sized to your biggest real risk, not a rule of thumb. Whatever is truly spare can then work on beating inflation.

options.text: Keep all $200,000 in the business account. Clients are unpredictable.
options.feedback: You're fully ready for a shock, which is worth something. But money beyond your reserve loses buying power every year to inflation, cutting your **real return**.

cards.title: "Can be reached" is not the same as "worth the same".
body: Some investments can be sold any day but may be worth less on the day you need them. Money for the reserve bucket should be both reachable and stable.

Read the exit terms before chasing a rate: early withdrawal penalties, notice periods, minimum balances. And size buckets to your own business. A seasonal firm needs a bigger reserve than one with steady monthly contracts.

cards.title: Ask when you'll need it, then make the rest beat inflation.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Liquidity:** keep money you may need soon where you can reach it at full value. **Real returns:** money sitting still loses buying power, so spare cash should earn more than prices rise.
**Try it today:** write your monthly costs and your biggest single risk. Size a ready and reserve amount. Is anything left over doing nothing?
